pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 12–13 years

- **Topic:** Heart Structure & Double Circulation

- **Standards — UK (DfE):** Builds on the statutory KS2 requirement (Year 6) to "describe the functions of the heart, blood vessels and blood" within the circulatory system, developed at KS3 into heart structure and the double circulatory system (and completed at GCSE). (Heart chamber/valve detail is introduced at KS3 in most English schemes and is statutory content at GCSE.)

- **Standards — US (NGSS MS-LS1-3):** "[curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-LS1-3]" (circulatory named among the subsystems). NGSS frames circulation as a subsystem interacting with the respiratory and digestive systems rather than teaching chamber anatomy explicitly.

- **Operational details:** Children label the heart (right and left atria and ventricles, valves, aorta, vena cava, pulmonary artery and vein, coronary arteries) and trace the route of blood through a DOUBLE circulation: body → right side → lungs (pick up O₂, drop CO₂) → left side → body. They explain valves preventing backflow and the left ventricle's thicker wall (pumps further, to the whole body), and compare arteries (thick, elastic, high pressure), veins (valves, low pressure) and capillaries (one-cell walls for exchange). The move that matters is grasping WHY circulation is double: blood is re-pressurised by the heart between the lung loop and the body loop, so it reaches the body at high pressure after being oxygenated.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B→C. Depends on the KS2 circulatory overview and gas exchange; a high-centrality hub linking transport to respiration and gas exchange. A child is secure when they can trace a blood drop through both loops in order and explain why the two circuits and the valves are needed.
bestPractices: Teach circulation by tracing a blood drop through the whole route, so the double-loop structure is experienced as a journey, not memorised as a diagram.
Make the PURPOSE of double circulation explicit — the heart re-pressurises blood between the lung loop and the body loop — rather than just naming two circuits.
Link oxygenation state to the loop (deoxygenated on the right/to lungs; oxygenated on the left/to body) and correct the 'heart oxygenates blood' error.
Tie structure to function: thicker left ventricle wall, valves preventing backflow, and artery/vein/capillary differences all explained by their job.
Use consistent colour convention (blue deoxygenated, red oxygenated) but note it represents oxygenation, not actual blue blood.
keyRepresentations: Labelled heart diagram (chambers, valves, great vessels, coronary arteries)
Double-circulation loop diagram (body loop and lung loop meeting at the heart)
commonMisconceptions: Thinking the heart adds oxygen to blood (the lungs do; the heart pumps).
Believing blood flows in a single loop rather than two circuits through the heart.
Thinking blue-drawn blood is literally blue rather than deoxygenated (dark red).
Confusing arteries and veins by oxygenation (the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood).
Assuming all chambers have equal muscular walls, missing why the left ventricle is thickest.

learn.summary: For ages 12–13, teach heart structure and double circulation by having learners trace a single blood drop through both the lung loop and the body loop, grasping WHY the circuit is double: the heart re-pressurises blood between the two loops so oxygenated blood reaches the body at high pressure. Core objectives: label the heart (atria, ventricles, valves, aorta, vena cava, pulmonary artery and vein, coronary arteries), explain how valves prevent backflow, explain why the left ventricle wall is thickest, compare arteries/veins/capillaries, and correct the error that the heart (rather than the lungs) oxygenates blood. Crucially, arteries and veins are defined by DIRECTION of flow (away from vs toward the heart), not by oxygenation — the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood and the pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood.

activities.title: Drive the blood: tracing one drop through two loops
feedback: If a learner routes blood from the lungs straight to the body, note that oxygenated blood returns to the LEFT side of the heart first and is re-pumped — that re-pressurising is the point of the second loop.
If a learner says the heart adds oxygen to the blood, correct: the lungs load the oxygen; the heart only pumps.
If a learner attributes pumping to the valves, clarify that valves only stop backflow — the muscular ventricle walls contract to pump.
If a learner treats the colour as literal, remind them it represents oxygenation state; deoxygenated blood is dark red, not blue.
activities.rationale: Tracing a drop makes the two-loop structure a journey with causal logic rather than a diagram to memorise, and a live pump/valve mechanism (clickable pumping, a visible valve that snaps shut on backflow, and a pressure readout on the left ventricle) makes valve function and re-pressurisation concrete. Comparing against a single-loop model surfaces the purpose of the second circuit.
sourceClaims: Humans have a double circulatory system: the right side pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs and the left side pumps oxygenated blood to the body; valves prevent backflow and the left ventricle has a thicker muscular wall to pump blood around the whole body.
learnerActions: Pump the heart and follow one blood drop all the way round, starting from the body: body → vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → to the lungs → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → back to the body.

Watch (or mark, on paper) the drop's oxygenation change: it loads oxygen in the lungs (deoxygenated → oxygenated) and unloads it as body cells use it (oxygenated → deoxygenated) — note that colour represents oxygenation state, not literally blue blood.
Try to push blood backwards through a valve and observe that a valve blocks it.

Compare the two circuits with a 'single circulation' model version: route blood straight from the lungs to the body without an intermediate return to the heart, and describe what happens to its speed and pressure by the time it reaches the body.
State in one sentence WHY mammals use a double circuit, referring to the heart re-pressurising blood between the lung loop and the body loop.
activities.intendedInsight: Double circulation is a routing process: blood passes through the heart twice per full circuit, and the heart re-pressurises it between the lung loop and the body loop so it reaches the body at high pressure after being oxygenated. Valves prevent backflow; the pumping force comes from heart muscle, not valves.

activities.title: Heart anatomy: chambers, valves and vessels in three dimensions
feedback: If a learner assumes all chambers have equally muscular walls, point to the relative wall thickness and ask which chamber pushes blood furthest.
If a learner thinks blood mixes across the heart, point to the septum dividing the two sides in a healthy heart.
When labelling, if 'artery = oxygenated' is applied to the pulmonary artery, flag it for the direction-based definition activity.
activities.rationale: A three-dimensional, manipulable heart shows the spatial arrangement of chambers, valves and great vessels and the relative wall thicknesses more directly than a flat diagram; rotating, cross-sectioning and animating a beat make the anatomy inspectable. A tappable labelled diagram (e.g. tap the left ventricle to reveal 'thickest wall — pumps to the whole body', tap a valve to reveal 'stops backflow') is an efficient naming scaffold, though static diagrams do not show flow dynamics.
sourceClaims: Humans have a double circulatory system: the right side pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs and the left side pumps oxygenated blood to the body; valves prevent backflow and the left ventricle has a thicker muscular wall to pump blood around the whole body.
learnerActions: Examine and rotate a manipulable heart model (a rotatable screen model, or a real sheep/pig heart), identifying the four chambers, valve positions and the great vessels in their spatial arrangement.
Cross-section the heart to compare the thickness of the left ventricle wall against the right ventricle and the atria.
Explain why the left ventricle wall is thickest by linking it to its job: pumping blood the whole way round the body.
Locate the septum and state what it does: keeps the oxygenated (left) and deoxygenated (right) blood from mixing in a healthy heart.
Label a diagram with atria, ventricles, valves, aorta, vena cava, pulmonary artery, pulmonary vein and coronary arteries.
activities.intendedInsight: Structure follows function: the four-chambered pump is spatially arranged so the two sides stay separate (septum), and the thicker left ventricle wall matches the greater pumping demand of the whole-body loop.

activities.title: Which way does water pass? Predict–observe with a valve
feedback: If the prediction and observation disagree, ask the learner to describe the valve's shape and how flow in one direction opens it while flow the other way presses it shut.
If a learner says the valve pumps or sets the heartbeat, separate the two: muscle contraction supplies the force; the valve only controls direction.
For the leaky-valve discussion: a leaky valve lets some blood flow backward (reduced efficiency), whereas a failed pump means the force to move blood is lost — both are problems, but different ones.
Remind learners that a physical specimen or water model is an approximation: it shows valve directionality but will not reproduce living pressures or flow.
activities.rationale: A predict–observe–explain task with real water flow makes one-way valve function directly observable and confronts the 'valves pump' misconception through evidence rather than assertion.
sourceClaims: Humans have a double circulatory system: the right side pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs and the left side pumps oxygenated blood to the body; valves prevent backflow and the left ventricle has a thicker muscular wall to pump blood around the whole body.
learnerActions: Before pouring, PREDICT which direction water will pass freely through a one-way valve model (or a valve in a fresh sheep/pig heart) and which direction will be blocked, and explain why.
Pour water through the valve in each direction and OBSERVE which way flows and which way is stopped.
Reconcile prediction with observation, stating in your own words what the valve does and what it does NOT do (it does not pump).
Discuss: if a valve became leaky, what problem would that cause, and why is that different from the pump (muscle) failing?
activities.intendedInsight: Valves are passive one-way gates that prevent backflow; they are opened and closed by the pressure of blood the muscle moves, not a source of pumping themselves.

activities.title: Defining arteries and veins by direction, not oxygenation
feedback: If a learner insists the pulmonary artery must carry oxygenated blood 'because all arteries do', show the route: it goes FROM the heart TO the lungs to collect oxygen — so the blood in it has not yet been oxygenated.
If a learner is unsure how many times a cell passes through the heart, have them retrace both loops: once before the lung loop and once before the body loop.

Reinforce that the direction-based definitions work for the circulation studied here, while the oxygenation rule has a standing exception at the pulmonary vessels (and also at the umbilical vessels before birth).
activities.rationale: Directly confronting the pulmonary exception forces a correct, general definition and is the discriminating difference between surface memorisation and genuine understanding. Structure-to-function comparison of the three vessel types supports the broader transport concept.
learnerActions: State the common shortcut rule: 'arteries carry oxygenated blood, veins carry deoxygenated blood.'

Apply it to the pulmonary artery and pulmonary vein, then check the actual blood each carries: the pulmonary artery carries DEOXYGENATED blood (heart to lungs); the pulmonary vein carries OXYGENATED blood (lungs to heart).
Rewrite the definition so it never fails: an artery carries blood AWAY from the heart; a vein carries blood TOWARD the heart — regardless of oxygenation.

Compare artery, vein and capillary structure and link each to its job: arteries have thick elastic walls for high pressure; veins have thinner walls and operate at low pressure, and many veins (especially in the limbs) have valves to prevent backflow; capillaries have one-cell-thick walls for exchange.
Trace a red blood cell from the vena cava all the way round until it returns, counting how many times it passes through the heart (twice per full circuit).
activities.intendedInsight: Arteries and veins are correctly defined by direction of flow, not oxygenation; the oxygenation shortcut breaks precisely at the pulmonary vessels. Vessel structure matches the pressure and function of each.

activities.title: Check your understanding: sequence, match and explain
feedback: Correct route order: body → vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → body.

Diagnostic answer: the pulmonary vessels break the rule; the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood and the pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood; define an artery as carrying blood away from the heart and a vein as carrying it toward the heart.
If a learner orders a single loop missing the separate lung circuit, return them to the drive-the-blood trace to re-establish the two loops.
activities.rationale: Sequencing the route, matching vessels to features and explaining wall thickness are clean, high-value checks; the diagnostic prompt specifically discriminates direction-based understanding from the oxygenation shortcut. These recognition-and-short-explanation items check identification and brief reasoning and should follow, not replace, the construction and tracing activities.
sourceClaims: Humans have a double circulatory system: the right side pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs and the left side pumps oxygenated blood to the body; valves prevent backflow and the left ventricle has a thicker muscular wall to pump blood around the whole body.
learnerActions: Put the chambers and vessels in the order a blood drop passes through them on a full double circuit.
Match each vessel type (artery, vein, capillary) to its distinguishing feature.
Explain why the left ventricle wall is thicker than the other chambers' walls.

Answer the diagnostic: a student writes 'arteries always carry oxygenated blood, veins always carry deoxygenated blood' — name the one pair of vessels where this breaks down, explain why it is wrong there, and give the correct direction-based definition.
activities.intendedInsight: Secure understanding means ordering the double-loop route correctly, defining vessels by direction, explaining valves and the septum, and justifying the left ventricle's thicker wall by its workload.

constraints: A rotatable heart model and a labelled tappable diagram are naming/anatomy scaffolds: they are strong for identifying chambers, valves and vessels and for comparing wall thickness, but being static (diagram) or anatomy-focused (model) they do not themselves demonstrate the flow dynamics and re-pressurisation logic — pair them with a trace of the moving blood drop.
Colour coding (blue deoxygenated, red oxygenated) is a convention representing oxygenation state only; make explicit that deoxygenated blood is dark red, not literally blue.

Recognition and matching items check that learners can identify correct answers; they do not by themselves elicit independent construction of the double-loop explanation, so include at least one activity where learners trace and explain the route in their own words.

The 'single circulation' comparison is a teaching contrast to reveal the purpose of the second loop; present it as a model variation, not as a claim about any specific real organism's physiology without evidence.
A conversational/interview format is a poor fit for this routing-and-structure topic, which is better served by tracing and manipulating the system; it is not recommended as the main scaffold here.

When using a real sheep/pig heart or a water-and-valve model, treat the physical specimen as an approximation of the idealised pump; observed water flow demonstrates valve directionality but pressures and flow will not match living circulation.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The BBC Bitesize source supporting the double-circulation and valve/wall-thickness claims is marked verified:false in the source row; the direction-based artery/vein definition and the pulmonary exception are standard curriculum content but have not been independently re-verified here, and no source claim in the row directly supports that definition (activity 4 sourceClaims left empty).

The left-ventricle re-pressurisation framing is pedagogically standard, but the 'single circulation → slow, low-pressure' contrast is a didactic model and should not be read as a measured physiological result for any particular organism.

No sources in this row establish comparative efficacy or necessity of any one medium (2D trace vs 3D model vs diagram vs physical heart); claims that only one medium can teach a given point have been kept as scoped affordances/limits.

The corrected direction-based definition of arteries/veins is placed directly in a learner activity (not merely caveated), since the row's own assessment identifies the oxygenation-only rule as the critical misconception to fix.

Activity 1's first learner action simplifies the route as '…to the lungs…' whereas activity 4 gives the full route naming the pulmonary artery and pulmonary vein; this is an intentional scaffolding simplification, not an inconsistency.

assess.poeTask: Using a one-way valve model (or a valve in a fresh sheep/pig heart), ask students to PREDICT which way water will pass through and which way it will be blocked, and why. Pouring water and seeing it flow one direction but not the other makes valve function — preventing backflow — directly observable.
probeDeeper: Trace a red blood cell from the vena cava all the way round until it returns — how many times does it pass through the heart?
Why does defining an artery by 'oxygenated blood' fail at the lungs, but defining it by direction never fails?
What would happen to the blood if the wall between the two sides of the heart had a hole?
If a valve became leaky, what problem would that cause, and why isn't that the same as the pump failing?
assess.correctAnswer: The pulmonary vessels break the rule: the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood from the heart to the lungs, and the pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood from the lungs back to the heart. The correct definition is by direction — an artery carries blood away from the heart, a vein carries blood back toward it — regardless of whether the blood is oxygenated.

errorPatterns.pattern: Arteries always carry oxygenated blood, veins always deoxygenated
errorPatterns.nextMove: Redefine by direction: away from the heart = artery, toward the heart = vein. The pulmonary vessels are the standing exception to the oxygenation shortcut.
errorPatterns.distractor: The pulmonary artery must carry oxygenated blood, because all arteries do.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Applies the oxygenation rule to the pulmonary artery/vein and gets them backwards

errorPatterns.pattern: The heart is one pump and blood does a single loop
errorPatterns.nextMove: Double circulation: the right side pumps blood to the lungs, the left side pumps it to the body — blood passes through the heart twice per full circuit.
errorPatterns.distractor: Blood travels round the whole body in one single loop, through the heart just once.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes one circuit through the heart, missing the separate loop to the lungs

errorPatterns.pattern: Oxygenated and deoxygenated blood mix inside the heart
errorPatterns.nextMove: The septum keeps the two sides separate; oxygenated and deoxygenated blood do not mix in a healthy heart.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Talks as if all four chambers share the same blood

errorPatterns.pattern: Valves pump the blood / control the heartbeat
errorPatterns.nextMove: Valves only prevent backflow; the pumping force comes from the heart muscle contracting.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Attributes pumping to the valves rather than to muscle contraction

responseLevels.gap: Relies on the oxygenation rule, describes a single loop, and can't handle the pulmonary vessels.
responseLevels.full: Defines arteries/veins by direction (resolving the pulmonary exception), traces the double circulation, explains valves prevent backflow and the septum keeps blood unmixed.
responseLevels.partial: Labels the heart and traces flow but still gets the pulmonary artery/vein wrong, or is shaky on why there are two separate loops.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A student writes the rule: 'arteries always carry oxygenated blood, veins always carry deoxygenated blood.' There is one pair of vessels where this rule breaks down. Which vessels are they, why is the rule wrong there, and what is the correct way to define what an artery does?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who truly understands defines arteries and veins by direction of flow and can name the pulmonary exception. A child relying on the memorised oxygenation rule gets the pulmonary vessels wrong.

sources.claim: The statutory KS2 (Year 6) programme requires pupils to 'describe the functions of the heart, blood vessels and blood' — the foundation KS3 develops into heart structure and double circulation.

sources.claim: NGSS MS-LS1-3 names the circulatory system among the interacting body subsystems students argue about.

Humans have a double circulatory system: the right side pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs and the left side pumps oxygenated blood to the body; valves prevent backflow and the left ventricle has a thicker muscular wall to pump blood around the whole body.
